OpenClaw hit 247K GitHub stars in under 60 days. Security researchers found 512 vulnerabilities in the same window - 8 critical. 🔴

The assertSandboxPath TOCTOU race condition can't be properly fixed in Node.js, and the /tools/invoke endpoint ignores the deny list entirely, so each patch leaves another path open.

ClawArmor enforces security at the Linux kernel syscall level, where OpenClaw can't override it regardless of configuration or injected instructions.

🔵 Three enforcement layers:
 ↳ Filesystem: workspace-only access, credential paths denied at kernel level
 ↳ Process: signed binary allowlist, nmap/curl/bash blocked before execution
 ↳ Network egress: allowlist-only outbound, exfiltration attempts denied and alerted

820+ malicious skills confirmed on ClawHub out of ~10,700. 
53,000+ instances exposed on the public internet with no authentication. Each one is a live agent with shell, filesystem, and network access and no kernel-level boundary.

🚨 How the TanStack npm attack actually happened:

1. Attacker opened a normal-looking pull request (#7378) on the TanStack repo.
2. GitHub automatically ran CI tests on that PR.
3. Code inside the PR stole the workflow's GitHub Actions Cache write token during the test run.
4. The attacker used that token to plant poisoned files in the shared build cache. The PR could be closed afterwards. The poisoned cache stays.
5. The official release workflow later pulled from the cache, baked the malicious files into the build, and signed and published 84 malicious package versions to npm.

Read more here: https://lnkd.in/g88bDzC9

We spent decades coming up with better alternatives to firewalls
But to secure agents you’re still opting for firewalls 😱 

I don’t like FW for AI because it introduces another hairpin and point of failure into an already fragile 3rd provider external network-reliant architecture.

Considering that most agent architectures call 3rd party LLMs, the trace where a users interacts with an agents that calls a third-party tool looks like this:

User ➡️  Agent ➡️  LLM ➡️  Agent ➡️ Proxy ➡️  3rd Party tool ➡️  Proxy ➡️  Agent ➡️  User


If you self-host the LLM and enforce security out-of band, you get this:

User ➡️  Agent/LLM ➡️  3rd Party tool ➡️  Agent/LLM ➡️  User


There are other limitation with inline enforcement, e.g. cannot see inside the execution environment like what libraries an agent loads, what system calls it makes, etc.

I understand big hairpin vendors rebranding their products for AI purposes, like Zscaler NetScaler Netskope Cato Networks

But why would startups go for an firewall-first architecture? Why would Palo Alto Networks acquire Portkey to turn it into a firewall?


I’ve got 2.5 out-of-band options and 1.5 acceptable in-band option for you:


💳 In-line credential-scoped enforcement

A lightweight synchronous query to a local policy engine before the agent acting, receiving allow/deny without routing the full payload through an external network boundary.

Examples include Token Security, Assury, Teleport, Permit0


🏃 Runtime Environment
Out-of-band sensors observe what the agent actually does at the kernel, process, or application level during execution, detecting and responding to behavioural anomalies without sitting in the request path.

ARMO, AccuKnox, Raven.io, Miggo Security, Sweet Security, Oligo Security


📦 Sandbox
Agent-generated code executes in an isolated environment (microVM, virtual kernel, hardened container) before reaching production, containing blast radius without inspecting the content of LLM requests.

E2B, Daytona, Northflank, BoxLite, Novita AI


↔️ Decoupled Control/Data Plane
Policy management and enforcement are architecturally separated, so access decisions either block execution locally with minimal overhead (Bucket 2) or propagate asynchronously through a separate signal channel without touching the agent's execution path at all (Bucket 3).

CrowdStrike's SGNL Obsidian Security, Permit.io, Cerbos, Galileo.ai

Funnily enough, I don’t get (or like) explicit zero trust products like ZTNA, because ZT will always end up being the outcome. 

What you need to do instead is to define smarter and more frictionless ways of reaching that zero trust sweet spot.

Here are the four natural ways I could fit in a silly graphic to reach zero trust:

⬛ Obfuscate resources - you can't lateral move if the lateral move doesn't exist. Includes the likes of NetFoundry, Tailscale, and Twingate

✍ Learn production behavior - assuming you’re not already compromised, you can monitor how your environment behaves today, and then define policies. Some examples include Tigera, ARMO, Zero Networks and AccuKnox

🛑 Preventative policies - these guys looked at your cloud environment configuration to determine whether your effective policies expose you to any attacks, which you can get from Native, as well as Blast Security and Aryon Security

👮 Policy decision points - paritcularly important for agent actions, these evaluate an action against a set of policies to allow/deny/alert/escalate. Some folks include Teleport, Cerbos, P0 Security, and Permit.io
